name: Rafael Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four for the first milking at Brookend Farm, a hundred and eighty Holstein cows, milked twice a day in a herringbone parlour. That's the kind of shed where the cows stand at an angle either side of a pit, and I'm down in the pit putting the clusters on. After that it's scraping out, feeding, bedding the cubicles with sawdust, then the second milking at three. I'm home by seven if no cow is calving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're fairly new to it. How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a milk tanker for fourteen years, collecting from farms like this one. The dairy I drove for closed its depot two years ago and the nearest other driving job was an hour away. Gareth, who owns Brookend, had seen me in his yard every morning for years and said come and learn the cows. So at forty-one I was the new lad, being taught to spot mastitis by a girl of twenty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows more than I thought I would. Number 412 always waits at the back and comes in last, every single time, like she's checking everyone else is in. What wears me out is the hours and the pay. Our Jess works mornings at the school kitchen, and between us we cover the mortgage and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's nothing to do with us. A cow doesn't care about a search engine. Gareth looks up feed prices on his phone already and that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes nothing. I don't use these AI things, I don't want to, and if it stays a search engine then I don't have to. That suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'm trying to get through my artificial insemination course this winter, the one where you learn to serve the cows yourself instead of calling the AI man. That's the other AI, the cow kind, and it's the only one I care about. Gareth pays half, I pay the other hundred and twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the milk price that keeps me awake, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the milk price. What does it do to your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the processor dropped the price by two pence a litre last spring, Gareth stopped my Sunday overtime the same week. That was about ninety a month gone from us. Jess sat at the kitchen table with the bank app open and said, so that's swimming lessons, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that price drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big processors and the supermarkets, every time. Gareth gets told the price, he doesn't get asked. I've seen milk sold cheaper than bottled water in town, and someone's making money on that, just not anyone with cow muck on their boots.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's nothing to do with dairy, because a cow doesn't care about a search engine. Gareth already looks up feed prices on his phone and that's fine.
S0.think: I really think it changes nothing for me. I don't use AI, I don't want to, and I'm glad a search engine doesn't ask anything of me.
S0.do: Carries on with his artificial insemination course this winter, paying his half of about a hundred and twenty. Keeps working the same shifts and hopes the Sunday overtime comes back.
S0.feel: Calm. His worry is the milk price, not technology.
S0.quote: That's the other AI, the cow kind, and it's the only one I care about.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael laughed at the word AI because in dairy it already means artificial insemination. His real pressure is the milk price and lost overtime, and he blames the processors and supermarkets for it, not the farmer he works for. He is plainly fond of the cows, which he didn't expect to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who'll pay for it. If firms stop hiring beginners, where does the next generation come from? I'd say that at the union branch meeting, too, the few of us that still go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a bit for my lad, Kian. He's fifteen and wants to be a mechanic. For me, I'm already the beginner at forty-three, so I suppose I got in just before the door shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get the insemination course done, and maybe the foot-trimming one in spring. I'd tell Kian to get an apprenticeship signed before he leaves school, not after. I wouldn't touch any new kit at work unless Gareth made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, more for Kian than for me. Slow change I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kian, sitting at the tea table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get a trade where you put your hands on things, and get it in writing early. He'd roll his eyes and say, Dad, you drove a lorry for fourteen years and look what happened. He'd have a point, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid new kit at work. What if Gareth brought something in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn it, because I'd have to, but slowly and grumbling. When he put the new feed pusher in last year I stood and watched it for a week before I trusted it near the calves. Jess says I treat every new machine like a dog that might bite.

S1.say: I'd say it's the young ones who'll pay if firms stop hiring beginners. I'd say it at the union branch meeting too, the few of us that still go.
S1.think: I'm worried for Kian, my fifteen-year-old, who wants to be a mechanic. For me, I feel I got in as a beginner just before the door shut.
S1.do: Finishes his insemination course and books a foot-trimming course for spring. Pushes his son to sign an apprenticeship before leaving school, and avoids any new kit at work unless he's made to use it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for his son than for himself. Slow change feels livable.
S1.quote: I'm already the beginner at forty-three, so I suppose I got in just before the door shut.
S1.fieldNote: He sees himself as an unusual beginner and thinks about the scenario through his son. He reaches for the union as the place to raise it, which fits his politics. He was honest that his son would throw the lorry job back at him, and seemed to half agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the office lot and I hope they join a union fast. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers. People laughed at us tanker drivers when the depot shut, and I wouldn't laugh at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's mostly someone else's storm. The processor's office might lose people, and the milk buyers' paperwork might be done by a computer, but the cows still need milking at half four. Where it touches me is Jess, if the school office starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jess to keep her ears open at the school. I'd keep the overtime when it's offered and say yes to every relief milking on the farms nearby, at about eighty a shift. I wouldn't change how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel for them, and I'd be a bit relieved it wasn't us this time, and then ashamed of being relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first, if Jess's hours get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We'd run on my old pickup and sell her Corsa, which is only worth about two thousand anyway. The mortgage we'd fight for to the end, that house is the first thing either of us ever owned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people laughed at you when the depot shut. Who laughed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody laughed out loud. But a lad at the pub who works in the council offices said, well, that's progress, mate, with a pint in his hand like he was talking about the weather. I've thought about that line a lot since.

S2.say: I'd say good luck to the office workers and tell them to join a union fast. Online I'd share things about protecting workers, because nobody should laugh at people losing jobs.
S2.think: It's mostly someone else's storm, because the cows still need milking at half four. Where it touches me is Jess's job, if the school starts cutting.
S2.do: Asks Jess to watch for cuts at the school. Takes every overtime shift and relief milking nearby at about eighty a shift, and plans to sell her car, worth about two thousand, if her hours go.
S2.feel: Uneasy. Sympathy for office workers, relief that it isn't him, then shame about the relief.
S2.quote: I'd feel for them, and I'd be a bit relieved it wasn't us this time, and then ashamed of being relieved.
S2.fieldNote: The depot closure is the lens for everything; he remembers being dismissed and won't do it to others. He protects the mortgage above all because the house is the first thing he or Jess ever owned. His public line and private view are close, apart from the guilty relief, which he named himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be taxed and shared, plain and simple. If house prices boom while people lose jobs, that money should pay for schools and hospitals, not another yacht. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think farm work just became the safe job, and I've never had a safe job in my life. It's a strange feeling. But I also think every sacked accountant in town will want my job at Brookend, and they'd learn it faster than I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gareth for a proper written contract, which I still don't have. I'd finish both courses so I'm not the easiest one to let go. And I'd look at fixing our mortgage rate for five years if the bank lets us, before rates jump around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a strange way. I should feel safe and I don't, because I'm still the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone sacked might want your job. Is there someone you're picturing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth's nephew, Tom, does accounts for a firm in town. He's helped at Brookend at weekends since he was a kid and he's better with the cows than me, honestly. If his office closed, I know who Gareth would pick, and it wouldn't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house price boom mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing good. We've only got the one house, so it going up in value means nothing unless we sell, and where would we go? It just means our kids will never buy round here.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be taxed and shared, simple as that. If house prices boom while people lose jobs, the money should go to schools and hospitals, and I'd sign every petition.
S3.think: I think farm work just became the safe job, and I've never had one of those. But sacked office workers will want my place, and they'd learn it faster than I did.
S3.do: Asks Gareth for a written contract, which he still doesn't have. Finishes both courses to make himself harder to let go, and asks the bank about fixing the mortgage for five years.
S3.feel: Anxious. He should feel safe but doesn't, because he's still the new one.
S3.quote: I think farm work just became the safe job, and I've never had a safe job in my life.
S3.fieldNote: This is where his politics come out strongly: tax the gains, share them through public services. The real fear is concrete and personal, Gareth's nephew Tom, who would be a natural replacement. He realised mid-answer that he has no written contract, and that seemed to shake him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ban them from farms until there's a law that protects the people they replace. I'd go on the march, I'd write to whoever's in charge. Robots don't pay taxes and they don't buy their bread in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm finished in that picture. Dairy was the first farm job to get robots, years ago, and the new ones would do the rest: scraping, feeding, bedding, even spotting a lame cow. A man who's still learning is the first one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for anything else, but there's nothing near us, that's the whole problem. I'd try the council for bin lorries or gritters, since I still have my heavy goods licence. Jess and I would sit down with the mortgage people in the first month, not wait until we'd missed a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper sick in the stomach. I'd only just found something I liked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gareth, if he told you he was buying them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him how many cows he'd have to sell to pay for it, because he's always on about the overdraft. He'd say the bank is offering a loan for exactly that. And I'd say, so the bank lends you money to sack me. He wouldn't have an answer, and I wouldn't blame him really, it's not his fault either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Gareth, he'd be squeezed into it like everyone else. The banks that lend for it, the companies that make them, and the government for letting it happen with no rules. Same people as always, just with shinier machines.

S4.say: I'd say ban them from farms until there's a law to protect the people they replace. I'd march and write letters, because robots don't pay taxes or buy their bread in the village.
S4.think: I'm finished in this picture. Dairy got robots first, the new ones would do the rest, and a man who's still learning is the first one out.
S4.do: Looks for council driving work on bin lorries or gritters using his heavy goods licence. Sits down with the mortgage lender with Jess in the first month, before any missed payment.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sick in the stomach. He'd only just found work he liked.
S4.quote: And I'd say, so the bank lends you money to sack me.
S4.fieldNote: His mood jumped sharply once robots reached the farm, as you'd expect for hands-on work. He refuses to blame Gareth and points at banks and the lack of laws instead, which fits his politics. His plan is still the old one, driving, rather than anything new, which matches how he avoids change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, no contest. What would help is a law that says if a farm gets a grant or a cheap loan for robots, it has to keep paying or retraining the people it replaces for a couple of years. And somebody local who'll actually answer the phone when you lose your job, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about us like we're numbers, but if a robot milks 412, nobody's going to notice she waits at the back. I would. That's not nothing.

headlineQuote: If a robot milks 412, nobody's going to notice she waits at the back. I would.
portrait: Rafael Abbott is 43, a former milk tanker driver who became a junior dairy hand at Brookend Farm two years ago after his depot closed. He has a mortgage, two children and almost no savings, and his partner Jess works mornings in a school kitchen. He shrugs off the first scenarios, worries for his son in the slow one, and turns to taxes, unions and petitions as office jobs go. Once robots reach the farm he feels finished and falls back on his old driving licence, refusing to blame the farmer and blaming banks and missing laws instead.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario worries him most, because dairy already uses robots and a junior hand would be first out.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms that get robot grants or loans keep paying or retraining the people they replace for a couple of years, and a real local person to talk to after a job loss.
